**Surah "Al-Mumtahanah"**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is narrated that a freedwoman of Abu 'Amr ibn Sayfi ibn Hashim, called Sarah, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Medina while he was preparing for the conquest (of Mecca). He said to her: "Have you come as a Muslim?" She said: "No." He said: "Have you come as an emigrant (muhajirah)?" She said: "No." He said: "Then what has brought you?" She said: "I am in dire need." So he urged the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib to help her, and they clothed her, provided her mount, and supplied her with provisions. Then Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah came to her, gave her ten dinars, clothed her in a cloak, and asked her to carry a letter to the people of Mecca. Its text was: "From Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to the people of Mecca: Know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intends to march against you, so take your precautions." Sarah set out, but Jibril (peace be upon him) brought the news to the Prophet ﷺ. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Ali, 'Ammar, 'Umar, Talhah, al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad and Abu Marthad, and they were horsemen. He said: "Go until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a woman riding with a letter from Hatib to the people of Mecca. Take it from her and let her go; but if she refuses, strike off her neck." They overtook her, but she denied (having it) and swore an oath. They were about to turn back, but 'Ali said: "By Allah, we have not been lied to, nor has the Messenger of Allah ﷺ been lied to!" He drew his sword and said: "Bring out the letter, or we will strike your head." So she brought it out from the braids of her hair.

It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted amnesty to all the people on the day of the conquest, except four, and Hatib was one of them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned Hatib and said: "What led you to do this?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have not disbelieved since I embraced Islam, nor have I deceived you since I gave you counsel, nor have I loved them since I parted from them. But I was a man attached to Quraysh, not one of their own clan, and all of those with you among the emigrants have relatives in Mecca who protect their families and property, whereas I have none. So I feared for my family, and I wished to gain a favour from them. I knew that Allah would send down His punishment upon them, and that my letter would not avail them anything." The Prophet ﷺ accepted his statement and his excuse. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "What would make you know, O 'Umar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said to them: 'Do what you will, for I have forgiven you.'" Then the eyes of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) overflowed, and there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾.

The verb "ittakhadha" (to take) is transitive to its two objects, which are "'aduwwi" (My enemy) and "awliya'" (allies). "Al-'aduww" (the enemy) is of the pattern "fa'ul", from "'ada", like "'afuww" from "'afa", but it is in the form of a verbal noun, so it is applied to the plural just as it is applied to the singular. In this is evidence that a major sin does not strip a person of the name of faith.

﴿Tulqūna﴾ (you convey) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "la tattakhidhū" (do not take). The meaning is: "Do not take them as allies, conveying affection to them." Or it is a new sentence after a pause, serving as a rebuke. The word "ilqa'" (conveying) means delivering affection to them and disclosing it to them. The preposition "bi" in "bil-mawaddah" (with affection) is superfluous (za'idah), emphasizing the transitivity, as in His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Or it is retained, with the object of "tulqūna" omitted, meaning: "You convey to them the news of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because of the affection between you and them."

﴿Wa-qad kafarū﴾ (while they have disbelieved) is a circumstantial clause either of "la tattakhidhū" or of "tulqūna", meaning: "Do not befriend them, or show them affection, while this is their state."

﴿Bi-mā jā'akum mina al-ḥaqq﴾ (in what has come to you of the truth): the religion of Islam and the Qur'an.

﴿Yukhrijūna al-rasūla wa-iyyākum﴾ (they expel the Messenger and you): this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining their disbelief and their defiance, or it is a circumstantial clause of "kafarū".

﴿An tu'minū﴾ (because you believe): this is the reason for "yukhrijūna", meaning: they expel you from Mecca because of your faith.

﴿Bi-llāhi rabbikum in kuntum kharajtum﴾ (in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone forth): this is connected to "la tattakhidhū", meaning: do not befriend My enemies if you are (truly) My friends. The grammarians' statement regarding such a construction is that it is a conditional clause whose response (jawab) is omitted, the preceding clause indicating it.

﴿Jihādan fī sabīlī﴾ (striving in My way): a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: if you have gone forth as strivers in My way.

﴿Wa-ibtighā'a marḍātī﴾ (and seeking My pleasure): meaning, and seeking My pleasure.

﴿Tusirrūna ilayhim bil-mawaddah﴾ (you confide to them with affection): meaning, you secretly disclose to them your affection; or, you confide to them the secrets of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because of the affection. This is a new sentence (isti'naf).

﴿Wa-anā a'lamu bi-mā akhfaytum wa-mā a'lantum﴾ (And I know best what you conceal and what you disclose): the meaning is: "What benefit is there for you in your secret dealings, when you know that concealing and disclosing are the same in My knowledge, and that I inform My Messenger of what you confide?"

﴿Wa-man yaf'alhu﴾ (And whoever does it): that is, this secret dealing.

﴿Minkum faqad ḍalla sawā' al-sabīl﴾ (among you, has indeed strayed from the right way): he has indeed erred from the path of truth and correctness.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 2:

﴿If they gain the upper hand over you⁠﴾, that is, if they prevail over you and gain control over you,

﴿they will be your enemies﴾, with utter enmity, and they will not be your allies as you are [to them],

﴿and they will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil﴾, with killing and reviling,

﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾, and they wish that you would apostatize from your religion. So, to show affection to such people is a great error on your part. And the past tense (al-madi) – although in the conditional construction (bab al-shart) it is treated in the manner of the present tense (al-mudari') – carries a subtle point here, as if it were said: they wish, before anything else, for your disbelief and your apostasy. That is, they want to inflict upon you the harms of this world and of religion, such as killing souls and tearing apart honour; or: your return to disbelief is the foremost of the harms in their eyes and the first of them, because they know that religion is dearer to you than your lives, since you expend your lives for its sake. The enemy's greatest concern is to target what is most important to his adversary.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 3:**

﴿Your relatives (arḥām) will not benefit you﴾, meaning your kinship ties (qarābāt),

﴿nor your children﴾, those for whose sake you befriend the disbelievers and draw near to them out of protectiveness toward them. Then He said: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you﴾, and between your relatives and your children,

﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [ʿAbasa 80:34], and so on. So why do you abandon the right of God for the sake of respecting the right of one who will flee from you tomorrow?

"Yafṣilu" (يَفْصِلُ) is the reading of ʿĀṣim. "Yufaṣṣilu" (يُفَصِّلُ) is the reading of Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, and the speaker is God, Mighty and Majestic. "Yufaṣṣalu" (يُفَصَّلُ) is the reading of Ibn Dhakwān. Others read "yufṣalu" (يُفْصَلُ).

﴿And God is Seeing of what you do﴾, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 4:

﴿There has indeed been for you an excellent example﴾, a model (qudwah) in disavowing one's kin,

﴿in Abraham﴾, that is, in his statements. For this reason he made an exception from it: "except the statement of Abraham,"

﴿and those who were with him﴾, of the believers. It was also said: they were prophets.

﴿When they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you﴾, the plural of "barī'" (free, innocent), like "ẓarīf" (witty) and "ẓurafā'" (witty people).

﴿and of what you worship besides Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity﴾, through actions,

﴿and hatred﴾, in the hearts,

﴿forever, until you believe in Allah alone.﴾ At that point we will abandon our enmity toward you.

﴿except the statement of Abraham to his father: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, and that was because of a promise he had made to him. That is, follow him in his statements, but do not emulate him in asking forgiveness for his disbelieving father.

﴿"And I have no power for you against Allah in anything."﴾ That is, in guidance, forgiveness, or success. This sentence is fitting for the exception. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Say, "Who then can prevent Allah for you of anything?"﴾ [al-Fath: 11]? But the intended meaning is the exception of the sentence "to his father," and the aim is the promise of asking forgiveness for him, while what follows is subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and within my capacity is only asking forgiveness."

﴿"Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾, connected to what precedes the exception, and it is part of the excellent example. It was also said: its meaning is, "Say: Our Lord," so it is the beginning of a command from Allah to the believers to say it.

﴿"And to You we have turned in repentance﴾, we have turned (aqbalnā),

﴿and to You is the final return.﴾ the destination (al-marji').

"Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve" (rabbana la taj'alna fitnatan lilladhina kafaru). Meaning: do not give them power over us, so that they subject us to torment through them.

"And forgive us, our Lord. Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise" (waghfir lana rabbana innaka anta al-'Aziz al-Hakim). Meaning: the Victorious, the Judge.

(p-469) ﴿Indeed, there has been for you in them an excellent example for whoever was hoping for Allah and the Last Day﴾. Then he repeated the exhortation to take Abraham (peace be upon him) and his people as an example, as confirmation and emphasis upon them. For this reason it was introduced with an oath, since that is the utmost in emphasis. And he replaced his words "for you" with his words "for whoever was hoping for Allah", i.e., His reward, meaning: fearing Allah. He followed it with His words: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾, i.e., turns away from Our command and takes the disbelievers as allies,

﴿then indeed Allah is the Free of need﴾, independent of the creation,

﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, the one deserving of praise. Thus He left out no kind of emphasis without bringing it. And when these verses were revealed, and the believers became severe in their enmity toward their fathers, their sons, and all their relatives among the polytheists, He gave them hope that the situation would change to its opposite, so He said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 7:

﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity.﴾ That is, from the people of Makkah, from your relatives,

﴿affection﴾, by guiding them to faith. When the conquest of Makkah was made easy, Allah granted them their wish, so their people embraced Islam, and mutual love was established between them. And "ʿasā" (it may be), is a promise from Allah, following the customs of kings, where they say concerning some needs: "ʿasā" or "laʿalla" (perhaps), so that the one in need is left with no doubt about its fulfilment. It is intended to give the believers hope,

﴿And Allah is All-Powerful﴾, over turning hearts, changing conditions, and facilitating the causes of affection,

﴿Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, toward those among the polytheists who embraced Islam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 8:

﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them.﴾ "Being righteous" means honouring them and doing good to them, in speech and in deed. The position (i'rab) of "an tabarruhum" (that you be righteous toward them) is genitive, in apposition (badal) to "alladhina lam yuqatilukum" (those who did not fight you). It is a badal ishtimal (an inclusive apposition), and the implied meaning is: "concerning the righteousness toward those who..."

﴿And act justly toward them﴾: deal with them justly in judgment, and do not wrong them. If He forbids wronging the polytheist, then how much more so with regard to the Muslim?! ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the just.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 9:

﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and assist in your expulsion, that you make allies of them﴾. It is a substitute (badal) for "those who fought you." It does not forbid you from showing kindness (mabarrah) to these people; rather, it forbids you from allying yourselves with (tawalli) these people,

﴿And whoever makes allies of them﴾ from among you,

﴿then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾, because they have placed alliance (tawalli) in other than its proper place.

﴿O you who have believed, when the believing women come to you﴾. He named them "believing women" either because they uttered the testimony of faith (kalimat al-shahadah), or because they are on the verge of their faith being confirmed through testing.

﴿emigrating﴾: accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

﴿So test them﴾: so try them by examining the signs, so that your conviction in the sincerity of their faith prevails. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Their testing is that she says: I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

﴿Allah knows best about their faith﴾: than you. Even if you examine their circumstances, you do not truly know that, but true knowledge of it belongs to Allah.

﴿If you know them to be believers﴾: the knowledge within your capacity, which is the predominant assumption (zann ghalib) arising from the apparent signs. Calling the assumption "knowledge" indicates that the predominant assumption, and what qiyas (analogical reasoning) leads to, takes the place of knowledge, and its holder is not included in His words: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ (17:36).

﴿then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾: do not send them back to their polytheist husbands.

﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾: meaning there is no lawful marital bond between a believing woman and a polytheist, because separation between them occurs when she emigrates as a Muslim.

﴿And give them what they have spent﴾: and give their husbands the equivalent of the bridal gifts (mahr) they paid. The verse was revealed after the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, and the treaty had stipulated that anyone among the people of Mecca who came to them as a believer would be returned. Allah then revealed this verse, clarifying that this applies to men and not to women, because a Muslim woman is not lawful to a disbeliever. It has also been said that this verse abrogated (naskh) the earlier ruling.

﴿And there is no blame upon you in marrying them﴾: then He removed the blame from them concerning marrying these emigrant women,

﴿when you have given them their wages﴾: meaning their bridal gifts, because the mahr is the wage for intimacy (ujr al-bud'). Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, used this as evidence that there is no waiting period (ʿiddah) upon the emigrant woman.

﴿And do not hold onto﴾: a Basran reading.

﴿the marriage bonds of disbelieving women﴾: al-ʿisma is that by which one holds fast, such as a contract or a cause. "Al-kawafir" is the plural of "kafirah," who is one who remained in the Abode of War (dar al-harb), or who joined the Abode of War as an apostate. That is, let there be between you and them no marital bond (ʿisma) and no conjugal tie. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "If a man had a wife in Mecca, he should not observe the waiting period on her account, because the difference of the two abodes has severed her marital bond with him."

﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾: from the bridal gifts of your wives who have joined the disbelievers, from whoever married them.

﴿And let them ask for what they have spent﴾: from the bridal gifts of their wives who emigrated, from whoever among us married them.

﴿That is the judgment of Allah﴾: meaning all that is mentioned in this verse.

﴿He judges between you﴾: this is a resumed statement, or a circumstantial clause (hal) of "the judgment of Allah," with the pronoun omitted, meaning "Allah judges," or "He made the judgment a judge," as an intensification. This ruling was abrogated, so no claim for the mahr remains, neither from us nor from them.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 11:

﴿And if any of your wives has escaped you to the disbelievers﴾, and if one of them has slipped away to the disbelievers, and in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "ahadun" (anyone),

﴿then you retaliate﴾, meaning you struck them in battle with a punishment, until you took spoils of war, according to al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, a grammarian and exegete),

﴿then give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent﴾, meaning give the Muslims whose wives have apostatized and gone over to the abode of war the bridal dowers of their wives from this spoil,

﴿and fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾. It was also said: this ruling has been abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) as well.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 12:**

﴿O Prophet, when the believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you,﴾ — this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿that they will not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children,﴾ — meaning the burying alive of daughters (wa'd al-banāt).

﴿nor bring a slander they have fabricated between their hands and their feet,﴾ — a woman would pick up a newborn and say to her husband, "This is my child from you." He (God) used "a slander fabricated between their hands and feet" as a metaphor for the child she attributes falsely to her husband, because the womb in which she carries it is "between the hands," and the place from which she gives birth is "between the feet."

﴿nor disobey you in what is right,﴾ — that is, in obedience to God and His Messenger.

﴿So accept their allegiance and ask God's forgiveness for them,﴾ — for what has passed.

﴿Indeed God is Forgiving,﴾ — by erasing what has gone before,

﴿Merciful,﴾ — by granting success in what is yet to come. It is related that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) finished, on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, taking the allegiance of the men, he began taking the allegiance of the women, while he was on al-Safa, and ʿUmar was sitting below him, taking their pledges on his behalf, by his command, and conveying [his words] to them. Hind bint ʿUtbah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, was veiled and disguised, fearing that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would recognize her because of what she had done to Ḥamzah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I take your pledge that you will not associate anything with God," and ʿUmar took the pledge of the women on that basis. Then he (ﷺ) said: "Nor steal." Hind said: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man, and I have taken some of his property, some trifles." Abu Sufyan said: "Whatever you have taken is lawful for you." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed and recognized her, and said to her: "Indeed, you are Hind." She said: "Yes. So pardon what has passed, O Prophet of God; may God pardon you." He said: "Nor commit adultery." She said: "Does a free woman commit adultery?!" He said: "Nor kill their children." She said: "We raised them when they were small, and you killed them when they were grown; you and they know best." Her son Ḥanzalah had been killed on the day of Badr. ʿUmar laughed until he fell backward, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) smiled. He said: "Nor bring a slander." She said: "By God, slander is indeed a shameful matter, and you only command us to what is right and to noble character." He said: "Nor disobey you in what is right." She said: "By God, we did not sit in this gathering of ours with the intention of disobeying you in anything."

It indicates that obedience to rulers is not obligatory in what is wrong (munkar).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 60, verse 13:

﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry﴾. He concluded the surah with what He began it with. It was said: they are the polytheists (mushrikun).

﴿They have despaired of the Hereafter﴾, of its reward, because they deny the resurrection (al-ba'th), (p-473) ﴿just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾, meaning: they have despaired. However, He put the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun.

﴿of the companions of the graves﴾, that they would return to them; or, just as their forebears who are in the graves have despaired of the Hereafter, meaning: these people are like their predecessors. It was also said: they are the Jews, meaning: do not take as allies a people who have incurred Allah's anger, who have despaired of having any share in the Hereafter because of their obstinacy toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), although they know in the Torah that he is the Messenger, just as the disbelievers have despaired of their dead being resurrected and returning to life. It was also said: "of the companions of the graves" is an explanation of "the disbelievers", meaning: just as the disbelievers who have been buried have despaired of the good of the Hereafter, because they have come to know the ugliness of their state and the evil of their final destination.
